tldr: This study scales latent world models on large-scale multi-embodiment real-robot data, showing that imagination error follows a second-order power law in compute, and that this error directly translates into downstream simulation and real-robot planning performance.
hero_caption: Overall architecture and training pipeline of RoboJEPA. Features from a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 visual encoder are sequenced alongside action and proprioceptive tokens to deterministically predict next-step latent states. The training incorporates both single-step prediction (Teacher Forcing) and autoregressive rollout prediction.
overview:
In large language models (LLMs), scaling laws predict how much model capabilities improve with increased compute and data, serving as a reliable roadmap for research and development. However, whether similar predictability holds for robotic world models that interact with the physical world has long remained an open question. Because robot data collection is exceptionally expensive, researchers urgently need principled metrics to decide beforehand how to allocate compute resources between model size and data volume.

To address this, the authors introduce RoboJEPA, an action-conditioned latent world model built upon the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), a self-supervised learning framework that predicts future states in feature space rather than pixel space. By unifying 23 large manipulation datasets spanning 12 robotic embodiments, they trained models ranging from 22 million up to 8 billion (8B) parameters. Rather than reconstructing pixels directly, RoboJEPA predicts future features within the latent space of a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder, allowing it to scale to unprecedented sizes with modest computational overhead.

Extensive evaluations show that latent rollout error on unseen data neatly follows a second-order power law in training compute. Crucially, improvements in this latent imagination error correlate strongly with higher success rates in downstream online planning tasks using single goal images, both in simulation (RoboCasa) and on real hardware (Franka/DROID). Consequently, researchers can now reliably predict downstream robot planning performance simply by observing offline latent prediction errors, without needing costly real-robot trial-and-error.
contributions: Building an 8B-parameter latent world model—the largest JEPA-based predictor to date—trained on a real-robot dataset mixture spanning 12 distinct embodiments.

Establishing scaling laws for robotic latent world models, demonstrating that imagination error follows a second-order power law in compute and enabling accurate extrapolation of large-scale model performance (4B, 8B) from smaller runs.
Demonstrating that offline latent prediction error serves as a remarkably reliable proxy for downstream goal-image planning performance in both simulation and the real world.

Showing that extending autoregressive rollout horizons during training significantly improves long-horizon planning scaling, uncovering a staged emergence of capabilities from end-effector control to complex object dynamics.

sections.heading: Turning Scaling into a Science: Does Robot Prediction Scale Predictably with Compute?
sections.summary: The authors ask whether scaling laws that revolutionized language and vision also hold for physical robot world models. By training RoboJEPA models from 22M to 8B parameters, they reveal that prediction error obeys a second-order power law and directly transfers to real-robot planning performance.
sections.details:
The remarkable progress in modern AI has been driven by the existence of scaling laws. Knowing beforehand how much performance will improve with additional compute allows researchers to logically budget model capacity and dataset size under finite resources. Yet, it was previously unknown whether such scaling laws apply to robotic latent world models—models that simulate environmental state transitions inside an abstract latent space rather than raw observation pixels.

Collecting real-world robotic data is notoriously labor-intensive and costly. Thus, having a scientific rule of thumb to decide how much compute to invest and how large a model should be for a given dataset was a critical missing piece. Prior world model works typically evaluated models at a single scale, leaving the relationship between compute and performance unstructured.

To close this gap, the authors developed RoboJEPA, which operates on the fixed representation space of V-JEPA 2.1. Across 23 public datasets spanning 12 robot embodiments and 26 action spaces, they trained model variants from 22M up to 8B parameters. The results demonstrate that latent rollout error on held-out data follows an exceptionally predictable second-order power law in compute, and that lowering this prediction error directly boosts downstream planning success rates on both simulated and real robotic platforms.

sections.heading: The RoboJEPA Design: Unifying Diverse Embodiments to Imagine Futures at Speed
sections.summary: RoboJEPA builds a Transformer-based deterministic predictor on top of a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. It handles data from 12 distinct robot platforms with varying camera setups, resolutions, and control rates in a unified structure, providing fast inference tailored for long-horizon planning.
sections.details:
### 2.1 RoboJEPA Architecture
The core philosophy of RoboJEPA is to forgo pixel-level reconstruction and instead deterministically predict how future feature representations evolve conditioned on robot actions in a single forward pass, operating within the latent space of a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder (patch embedding dimension $D_e=1664$). It uses a Vision Transformer backbone where each spatial input token predicts its corresponding spatial token at the subsequent timestep.

To support diverse embodiments and camera setups, several architectural components are introduced. First, a 4-axis Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) factorizes time, height, width, and viewpoint dimensions, allowing seamless interpolation and generalization across single- and multi-view setups as well as varying patch resolutions. Second, viewpoint types (such as wrist or static cameras) are injected as learnable biases. For training stability, QK-normalization and RMSNorm played indispensable roles.

The training objective balances two losses (Equation 4): a standard Teacher Forcing loss that predicts one-step-ahead features from ground-truth context tokens, and an Autoregressive Rollout loss where the model feeds its own predicted features recursively into the context, substantially mitigating exposure bias during inference.

### 2.2 Data, Training and Inference
The training corpus combines 23 public datasets across 12 robot platforms (single-arm, dual-arm, and humanoids), totaling 15,022 hours of video (with 6,692 hours of action-aligned data). To accommodate differences in control frequencies and action spaces (26 distinct spaces, ranging from 7-DoF delta end-effector poses to dual-arm and mobile bases), resampling and embodiment-specific action projection layers are utilized.

For inference and planning, the model employs the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM), a sampling-based trajectory optimization algorithm. Given a single goal image specifying the task outcome, CEM optimizes action sequences to minimize distance to the goal feature. To maximize inference throughput, RoboJEPA implements a rolling KV cache and Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) compilation via PyTorch Inductor into C++ artifacts, allowing the 8B model to execute multi-step planning within seconds.

### 2.3 Diffusion Decoder
To visually inspect latent predictions, the authors trained a dedicated Diffusion Decoder (an ~800M parameter DiT) that maps latent features back to RGB video. Combined with a Cosmos tokenizer, it reconstructs latent trajectories predicted at 5Hz into smooth 20 FPS videos. This decoder is strictly used for qualitative visualization and is completely bypassed during CEM planning.

captions.F3: The RoboJEPA training framework. The Teacher Forcing loss on the left learns accurate single-step transitions, while the autoregressive rollout loss on the right (leveraging a KV cache) imparts robustness against compounding prediction errors over long horizons.

sections.heading: Empirical Scaling Laws: Does Offline Imagination Error Predict Real-Robot Success?
sections.summary: Evaluations confirm that latent prediction error on unseen real and simulated data follows a second-order power law. Furthermore, downstream planning success rates scale predictably with compute, proving that offline error serves as a strong proxy for physical robot evaluation and revealing a staged emergence of physical capabilities.
sections.details:
### 3.1 World Model Scaling Laws
The authors evaluated the relationship between training compute (FLOPs) and latent prediction error (9-step rollout $L_1$ error) on held-out data. Comparing four functional forms—standard power law, second-order power law ($L(C)=A\,C^{\alpha-\gamma\ln C}+E$), BNSL, and UNSL—the second-order power law provided the most accurate extrapolation from smaller models (22M–2B) to larger scales (4B, 8B) (Table 2). This relationship held consistently across both real-world DROID and simulated RoboCasa datasets, delineating a clear compute frontier.

### 3.2 Downstream Planning Scaling
To verify whether offline prediction gains translate into online planning, basic goal-reaching tasks in RoboCasa were evaluated under a 1-step greedy CEM planner (reaching 3D end-effector poses and maintaining object grasp while reaching). Downstream success rates scaled smoothly as a power law in training compute. 3D end-effector control emerged around $10^{20}$ FLOPs, while grasp maintenance began improving around $3\times 10^{20}$ FLOPs (corresponding to 50M–100M parameter models).

### 3.3 Better Scaling for Long Horizon Planning
For non-greedy, long-horizon tasks requiring obstacle avoidance or object pushing, the initial model (trained with a short rollout horizon $K=2$) saw its scaling trend break down. Introducing a long-horizon training phase during the learning rate cooldown—increasing rollout length to $K=10$ and mixing in higher-resolution data—re-established smooth scaling in obstacle avoidance. In the object pushing task (Figure 15), success rates remained at zero until compute crossed roughly $10^{22}$ FLOPs (2B+ models). This demonstrates a hierarchical progression of capabilities: end-effector control $\to$ grasp maintenance $\to$ static geometry awareness $\to$ dynamic object interaction.

### 3.4 Real World Robotic Capabilities
On a physical Franka arm (DROID platform), RoboJEPA was evaluated across Grasp, Object Lift, and Pick and Place tasks using single goal images. Keeping planning hyperparameters identical across scales, success rates improved monotonically with model capacity (the 8B model achieved 90% in Grasp, 80% in Lift, and 53.3% in Pick and Place). In contrast, baseline VLA models ($\pi_0$-FAST and $\pi_{0.5}$) suffered catastrophic failures on specific tasks (e.g., 0% in Lift) due to language instruction priors, whereas RoboJEPA showed robust execution proportional to task complexity.

### 3.5 Qualitative Analysis
Decoding latent predictions back to pixel space using the Diffusion Decoder revealed that larger models accurately imagine physical contact between the gripper and objects, as well as complex deforming dynamics like cloth folding. Smaller models produce blurred rollouts where contact interactions dissolve.

sections.heading: Relation to Prior Work: Not Video Generation or Policy Learning, but Scaling Latent Dynamics
sections.summary: This work is contextualized among JEPA architectures, RL world models like Dreamer, VLA models like RT, and existing scaling law literature. RoboJEPA distinguishes itself by formulating scaling laws for latent dynamics rather than pixel rollouts or direct policy learning across diverse real-robot data.
sections.details:
Robotics foundation models take diverse forms, and RoboJEPA occupies a distinct niche at their intersection:

- **Lineage of JEPA Architectures**: JEPA (LeCun, 2022) discards pixel reconstruction to predict in an abstract latent space, evolving into I-JEPA and V-JEPA. While V-JEPA 2-AC (Assran et al., 2025) introduced action conditioning on small-scale robot data, RoboJEPA scales this concept across diverse multi-embodiment data up to 8B parameters and derives the first extrapolatable scaling laws.
- **Contrast with Video and RL World Models**: Frameworks like Dreamer (Hafner et al.) and recent video generation world models (Genie, UniSim, Cosmos) incur immense computational costs by simulating raw pixels. Operating in a frozen, pre-trained representation space makes RoboJEPA orders of magnitude faster to train and evaluate, enabling practical online CEM planning.
- **Contrast with Policy Scaling**: VLA models such as RT-1/2, OpenVLA, and $\pi_0$ directly learn behavioral policies via imitation learning (BC). In contrast, RoboJEPA models environment dynamics—how the world responds to actions. This grants it the flexibility to perform zero-shot planning toward arbitrary visual goals without task-specific policy tuning.
- **Scaling Law Formulations**: While scaling laws are well-studied in LLMs (e.g., Chinchilla) and vision models, this work is the first to establish a rigorous mathematical scaling formulation for action-conditioned robot world models that directly translates to physical hardware evaluation, providing a principled tool for model design.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Horizons: A New Frontier for Robot World Models
sections.summary: RoboJEPA demonstrates that latent world model imagination error follows a second-order power law and strongly correlates with physical planning success. Checkpoints and code are publicly released. Key limitations include relying on a frozen visual encoder and lack of natural language conditioning.
sections.details:
By training across large-scale datasets spanning 12 robot embodiments within the V-JEPA 2.1 latent space, this work introduces RoboJEPA, scaling action-conditioned latent world models up to 8B parameters. The authors prove that latent rollout errors obey a second-order power law with compute, and that this error serves as a dependable offline proxy for downstream planning performance in simulation and on real robots, bypassing the need for exhaustive real-hardware validation.

Furthermore, the findings reveal distinct compute thresholds required for physical reasoning to emerge—progressing from basic kinematic reaching to complex non-prehensile manipulation. To accelerate research, all model weights, training pipelines, and robot deployment scripts are released open-source.

Nonetheless, several limitations remain. First, because the visual encoder (V-JEPA 2.1) was kept frozen, joint scaling behaviors between encoder and predictor remain unexplored. Second, models were trained over multiple epochs on a fixed corpus, showing early signs of data saturation; further frontier expansion will require larger, more diverse interaction datasets. Third, task specification is currently restricted to single goal images, leaving natural language conditioning and policy prior guided sampling as exciting avenues for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix Highlights: Critical Implementation and Engineering Details
sections.summary: This section covers essential engineering choices detailed in the appendix: why V-JEPA 2.1 is critical over earlier versions, the mathematical formulation of 4-axis RoPE and view bias, and the AOT-compiled inference engine that enables real-time 8B planning.
sections.details:
The appendix provides several vital insights necessary for reproduction and real-world deployment:

- **Encoder Selection Matters (Appendix K)**: Early experiments using V-JEPA 2 suffered from training instability and divergence when scaling up. While V-JEPA 2 and 2.1 achieve similar global image classification scores, V-JEPA 2.1 provides vastly superior dense geometric representations (e.g., depth estimation and segmentation), which proved essential for scaling predictive physical dynamics.
- **4-Axis RoPE and View Bias (Appendix A)**: Attention head dimensions are split across four distinct rotary frequencies: time $t$, vertical coordinate $i$, horizontal coordinate $j$, and view index $v$. This allows the model to interpolate across variable numbers of cameras and patch resolutions without retraining. Additionally, a learnable view bias vector is injected into each layer to distinguish camera perspectives (e.g., wrist vs. static over-the-shoulder cameras).
- **High-Throughput Inference Engine (Appendix I)**: CEM planning requires thousands of forward passes at every control step. Profiling indicated that host-side dispatch overhead, rather than matrix multiplication, accounted for 31% to 47% of latency. Using PyTorch Inductor, the authors pre-compiled 54 static input shapes Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) into C++ shared artifacts with shared model weights. This slashed initialization startup times from 15–20 minutes down to just 1.2–1.5 seconds, enabling near-real-time planning on physical hardware.

takeaways: Robotic latent world models follow a predictable second-order power law in compute, allowing researchers to extrapolate large-scale model quality from small-scale training runs.
Offline latent rollout error ($L_1$ distance) acts as an exceptionally reliable proxy for downstream task success rates in both simulation and real-world robot planning.

Complex physical understanding (such as object dynamics) emerges only after crossing specific compute thresholds ($\approx 10^{22}$ FLOPs), and training with longer autoregressive horizons ($K=10$) is essential for unlocking it.
By predicting in latent feature space rather than pixel space and utilizing AOT-compiled execution, an 8B-parameter world model can plan on real hardware within practical timeframes.
limitations: The visual encoder is kept frozen while scaling only the predictor, leaving the dynamics of joint encoder-predictor co-scaling unaddressed.
Performance on the current data mixture shows signs of irreducible error and data saturation, meaning further scaling frontiers will demand larger and more diverse physical interaction datasets.
Task specification is limited to a single visual goal image, lacking support for natural language goals or policy priors to guide the sampling search.
